title: A correlation heatmap shows which parameters move together, and the blocks of red are the ones that cannot be treated independently
summary: Each heatmap is a symmetric table of Pearson correlations between reactions' parameters across all targets, one per Arrhenius parameter. Read the blocks, not the cells: a block of strongly positive cells means those reactions act as one group.

media.alt: A square heatmap of 18 by 18 Pearson correlation coefficients between n-heptane reactions for the pre-exponential parameter A, red for positive and blue for negative, colour bar from minus one to one, numbers printed in each cell. A cluster of dark red cells appears among the hydroperoxyl and methylperoxy hydrogen-abstraction reactions; one dark blue cell reads about minus 0.74.

source.caption: A-factor correlation heatmap
source.note: The page text says the correlations are estimated from sensitivity analysis; the figure itself is titled 'Reaction correlation across all targets' and does not state what is correlated. The explainer teaches the generic reading.

read_the_figure.question: Which pairs of reactions have parameters that vary together across the targets, and does that coupling differ between A, n and Ea?
read_the_figure.axes: Both axes list the same 18 reactions (n-heptane, as written on the figure) in the same order, so the matrix is symmetric about the diagonal. Each cell is a Pearson correlation r between the row reaction and the column reaction, coloured on a fixed diverging scale from minus 1 (dark blue) through 0 (white) to plus 1 (dark red). The number inside the cell is the same r.
look_at: The diagonal is 1 by definition (dark red): it carries no information.

Look for squares of dark red off the diagonal. In the A map and the Ea map the hydroperoxyl (HO2) abstraction reactions form such a block, with r about 0.8 to 0.9; in the Ea map the methylperoxy (CH3O2) pair is about 0.8.

Find the blue cells: the A map has a strongly negative cell of about minus 0.74 between a decomposition reaction and an OH abstraction reaction. A negative r means one goes up when the other goes down.
Compare the three maps. The row order is not the same in each, so compare reactions by name, never by position.
read_the_figure.proves: That the parameters of some reactions are strongly coupled across the targets, so they cannot be varied or sampled independently without ignoring a visible structure. It says nothing about causes.
if_wrong: A colour bar that is not symmetric around zero, or that stretches to the data range, exaggerates weak correlations.
A matrix whose rows are ordered differently from its columns cannot be read as symmetric.
Correlation from very few targets is unreliable: a value of 0.3 is not distinguishable from zero with a handful of points.
A strong correlation between two reactions can come from a shared third variable, not from direct coupling.
must_check: A symmetric colour scale centred on zero (here minus 1 to plus 1), with a labelled colour bar (here 'Pearson r').
Row and column order identical and chosen to reveal structure (here the order is not sorted by block, so blocks are scattered).
The number of samples behind each correlation is given. It is not stated on these figures.
What exactly is correlated (sensitivity coefficients, fitted values, samples) is stated in the title. Here the title says only 'across all targets'.
Cell numbers are legible: here they are very small.
as_drawn: Read by eye: HO2-abstraction pair in the A map about 0.9; most pairs between unrelated reaction classes are below 0.3 in magnitude.
A map: the most negative visible cell is about minus 0.74.
n map: the two CH3O2 abstraction reactions show about 0.98, the HO2 pairs about 0.9.
Ea map: the HO2 pairs about 0.89 and the CH3O2 pair about 0.83.
Each map has 18 reactions, so 18 x 17 / 2 = 153 distinct off-diagonal pairs.

terms.meaning: The covariance of two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations. It measures linear co-variation on a scale from -1 to +1.
A symmetric table of r for every pair of variables, with ones on the diagonal.
A colour scale with a neutral centre (here white at 0) and two hues for the two signs, so sign and strength are read at once.
The square of r is the fraction of one variable's variance that a straight-line fit on the other explains.

terms.term: Pre-exponential factor, temperature exponent, activation energy
terms.meaning: The three parameters of a modified Arrhenius rate: k = A T^n exp(-Ea / R T). The three heatmaps correspond to the three.
A group of variables that are all strongly correlated with each other, seen as a square of strong colour off the diagonal.
A strong r that arises from a common driver or from too few samples rather than from a direct link.

remember: r is symmetric: cell (i, j) equals cell (j, i). Half of the matrix is redundant.
r measures straight-line co-variation only. A curved dependence can have r near 0.
r squared is the shared-variance fraction: r = 0.9 shares 81 percent, r = -0.74 shares about 55 percent.
Correlation is not causation, and a correlation computed from few points is noisy.
A heatmap order that does not group related rows hides block structure: reorder before judging.

understand.title: Why three maps
understand.text: The rate of each reaction depends on three parameters (A, n, Ea), and a reaction's uncertainty in each can be coupled to other reactions in a different way. One map per parameter keeps those couplings separate; comparing them tells you whether the coupling you see in A also appears in Ea.

understand.title: Reading a block
understand.text: Reactions of the same type, for example abstraction of a hydrogen atom by the same radical from different sites of the same molecule, tend to form a block: they are chemically similar, so their parameters, or whatever is being correlated, move together. The block is the visible sign that treating them as independent would be wrong.

understand.title: What the picture cannot say
understand.text: A correlation matrix is a summary of pairs. It does not show whether three reactions move together as a trio, it does not say why, and it carries no uncertainty of its own. Treat strong cells as flags for closer study, not as results.

steps.title: Pearson correlation of two vectors
steps.note: The sum runs over the targets k. Dividing by the two spreads removes units, so every cell is on the same scale from -1 to 1.

steps.title: From covariance to correlation
steps.note: The correlation matrix is the covariance matrix rescaled by the standard deviations. It is the same information with the scales removed.

steps.title: Bounds and the diagonal
steps.note: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds every cell. The diagonal is always one, which is why it adds nothing.

steps.title: Shared variance
steps.note: For a straight-line fit of one variable on the other, r squared is the fraction of the total variance that the line explains.

steps.title: Number of distinct pairs
steps.note: For m = 18 reactions there are 153 pairs to read, which is why block structure matters more than individual numbers.

steps.title: Sampling noise of r
steps.note: A standard large-sample approximation: with few targets N, a printed r has an error bar of the same order as the weak correlations in the map. For r = 0 the error is about one over the square root of N - 1.

steps.title: Why correlation matters downstream
steps.note: The output variance of any linear combination contains cross terms. Ignoring a strong positive correlation understates the spread of a sum of the two parameters, and ignoring a strong negative one overstates it.

worked.title: What does r = -0.74 mean?
worked.problem: The A map shows r of about -0.74 between two reactions. What share of the variance of one is explained by the other, and which way do they move?

solution.text: Interpret: about 55 percent of the variance is shared, and the negative sign means one tends to rise when the other falls.

worked.answer: About 55 percent shared variance, in opposite directions. More than a coin flip, but far from deterministic: 45 percent of the variation is unexplained.

analyze.q: The HO2-abstraction reactions form a red block in the A map and in the Ea map. Give two different explanations for such a block and one comparison that could tell them apart.
analyze.hint: A direct coupling versus a common driver; look at whether the block also appears for n.

analyze.q: The row order differs between the three maps. What would you do to compare them fairly, and what could be hidden by the current order?
analyze.hint: Reorder all three by the same chemical class and look for the same block moving between maps.

analyze.q: One cell shows r = -0.74 and the colour is blue. What would you check before concluding that the two reactions are coupled?
analyze.hint: Number of samples, outliers, and a scatter plot of the two variables.

evaluate.q: Is a heatmap the best form here? List one thing it hides that a clustered, reordered map or a scatter matrix would show.
evaluate.hint: Block structure, nonlinear shapes, number of samples.

evaluate.q: Decide whether it is acceptable to sample these parameters independently. What minimum correlation would make you refuse, and why?
evaluate.hint: There is no universal threshold; relate it to how strongly the correlation changes the output variance.

create: Redraw the A map with rows and columns reordered into reaction classes, a diverging scale fixed at plus and minus 1, and the sample count in the title.
Design a figure that shows, for the strongest pair in each map, the scatter of the two parameters next to the r value.

checks.q: Why is the diagonal of a correlation matrix always 1?
checks.answer: A variable is perfectly linearly related to itself, so its covariance with itself equals the product of its standard deviations; the ratio is 1.

checks.q: A cell shows r = 0.9. How much variance do the two reactions share?
How many distinct off-diagonal pairs does an 18 by 18 correlation matrix hold, and why is that a problem for reading it cell by cell?
checks.answer: 18 x 17 / 2 = 153 pairs. Too many to read one at a time, so structure (blocks) has to carry the message.

checks.q: A map built from five targets shows r = 0.5 between two reactions. Is that evidence of coupling?
checks.answer: Not by itself. With N = 5 the error is about 0.75 / 2 = 0.38, so r = 0.5 is only about 1.3 error bars from zero.

checks.q: How would you make the block structure obvious?
checks.hint: Order the rows by something the blocks share.
checks.answer: Reorder rows and columns by reaction class or by hierarchical clustering on 1 - |r|, keep the diverging scale fixed at -1 to 1, and draw thin lines between the classes.
